original_question: How can one explain this phenomenon that the Euler class in H 2n (Homeo0 (S2n−1 )) is unbounded but it vanishes on amenable subgroups?
target_in_paper: Question 3.15 in Section 3.6 ("Amenable actions and planar groups and the Euler class").
correct_elements: Your draft correctly isolates the exact phenomenon highlighted in the paper: the universal Euler class for flat odd-sphere bundles is unbounded, yet its restriction to amenable subgroups vanishes. It also keeps the correct ambient group, namely Homeo_0(S^{2n-1}), and focuses on explaining that contrast rather than drifting to the separate noncompact R^{2n} problem.
missing_details: The nearby context makes clear that the unboundedness statement is for odd spheres S^{2n-1} with n > 1; this restriction should be stated.
The class in question is the universal Euler class of oriented flat S^{2n-1}-bundles, not an Euler class attached to one particular action.
To make the question stand-alone, the cohomology object should be specified explicitly, e.g. e_{2n} in H^{2n}(BHomeo_0(S^{2n-1}); Z) or equivalently group cohomology of Homeo_0(S^{2n-1}).
Homeo_0(S^{2n-1}) should be identified as the identity component of the homeomorphism group of S^{2n-1}.
The vanishing clause is universal: the restriction of the Euler class to every amenable subgroup vanishes, by the Hirsch-Thurston result cited in the surrounding text.
The paper's official formulation is broader than the first sentence alone: it explicitly asks whether this Euler class is hyperbolic in Gromov's sense.
The official formulation also asks a second concrete question about the volume-preserving subgroup Homeo_0^{vol}(S^{2n-1}).
For that second part, the coefficient field should be stated: the paper uses real coefficients.

If one says "bounded Euler class" in a stand-alone formulation, one should clarify that this means a bounded refinement/representative, i.e. a class coming from bounded cohomology via the comparison map.
The term "volume-preserving" should be tied to a fixed volume form on S^{2n-1}.
To stay paper-faithful, the sphere case should not be merged with the separate Question 3.16 about amenable C^1-actions on R^{2n}.
refined_question: For n > 1, let e_{2n} denote the universal Euler class of oriented flat S^{2n-1}-bundles, viewed as a class in H^{2n}(BHomeo_0(S^{2n-1}); Z), where Homeo_0(S^{2n-1}) is the identity component of the homeomorphism group of S^{2n-1}. Hirsch-Thurston implies that the restriction of e_{2n} to every amenable subgroup of Homeo_0(S^{2n-1}) vanishes, while bounded-cohomology methods show that e_{2n} is unbounded. How can this dichotomy be explained? More precisely, is e_{2n} hyperbolic in Gromov's sense, and, after passing to real coefficients and restricting to the identity component Homeo_0^{vol}(S^{2n-1}) of the homeomorphism group preserving a fixed volume form on S^{2n-1}, does the Euler class lie nontrivially in the image of the comparison map H_b^{2n}(BHomeo_0^{vol}(S^{2n-1}); R) -> H^{2n}(BHomeo_0^{vol}(S^{2n-1}); R)?
justification: The draft is aiming at Question 3.15: its opening sentence is almost exactly your wording. The surrounding paragraph in Section 3.6 supplies the missing scope: Hirsch-Thurston gives vanishing on amenable actions on spheres, and the bounded-cohomology discussion identifies the unboundedness phenomenon for the universal Euler class when n > 1. The official question then sharpens your draft in two precise directions: whether the class is hyperbolic in Gromov's sense, and whether there is a nontrivial bounded Euler class on the volume-preserving subgroup. I therefore kept the sphere/amenable-subgroup focus, added the universal-class and coefficient data needed to make the question self-contained, and avoided broadening it to the separate noncompact analogue of Question 3.16.
